title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)
version: Extended version published 2014-05-20 (USENIX ATC '14 paper plus extra material)
why: The canonical Raft description, whose Section 2 states the replicated state machine problem, Section 5.2 gives leader election with terms and randomized timeouts, and Section 5.6 states the broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF timing requirement.

title: Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (PhD dissertation)
version: Stanford University, August 2014; dissertation source commit 0c10ea1b (2016-05-24)
why: Ongaro's full dissertation gives the longer motivation and design rationale behind Raft, with Chapter 3 ('Basic Raft algorithm') covering terms, election rules and split votes, Section 3.8 persisted state and server restarts, and Section 3.9 the timing requirement.

title: Paxos Made Simple
why: Lamport's own short statement of the consensus problem and its safety conditions (Section 2.1, 'The Problem'), best for showing what any agreement protocol such as Raft must guarantee and how it differs from Paxos.

title: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process
version: Journal of the ACM Vol. 32, No. 2, April 1985, pp. 374-382
why: The classic impossibility proof that no deterministic asynchronous protocol can guarantee termination with even one crash-faulty process, which explains why Raft and Paxos give up guaranteed liveness and assume partial synchrony.

title: etcd-io/raft (Go Raft library)
why: The most widely deployed Raft implementation, where raft.go holds the follower/candidate/leader state machine, term handling and randomized election timeouts, and the README states exactly which state must be persisted and synced before messages may be sent.

title: fsync(2) - synchronize a file's in-core state with storage device
version: Linux man-pages 6.19-1 (2026-02-08); read locally as 'man 2 fsync'
why: Primary description of what fsync and fdatasync actually guarantee, including that a directory entry needs its own fsync and that some kernels and filesystems do not flush disk caches at all.

title: PostgreSQL 17 Documentation, 28.3. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
why: A production database explaining the write-ahead log idea, why only the WAL must be synced to commit a transaction, and how the log is replayed after a crash.

title: Atomic Commit In SQLite
why: Step-by-step account of a real journal-based commit, including SQLite's explicit hardware assumptions about sector writes and ordering, best for the durable-vs-volatile state and fsync-ordering part of the bridge chapter.
